analysis.one_liner: Taxes high wages and investment income to fund Social Security and Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill would add Social Security tax to wages up to $400,000, add a 1.2% Medicare tax above $400,000–$500,000, and roughly quintuple the investment-income tax rate on the richest estates, but since its May 8, 2025 introduction it has had no cosponsors and no action beyond referral to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises money for Social Security and Medicare by changing who pays federal payroll and investment taxes. Today, wages above roughly $176,000 pay no Social Security tax; the bill would apply the tax to wages between that cap and $400,000, and add a 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 ($500,000 for married couples). It also raises taxes on investment income for people making more than those thresholds — including income from businesses they actively own and some foreign income — and routes 71.3% of that money to Social Security's retirement fund, 10.3% to disability insurance, and 28.7% to Medicare's hospital fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries — current retirees, disabled workers, and future beneficiaries — gain because the new taxes flow directly into the trust funds that pay their benefits, extending the revenue available to them [S2]. Nearly everyone who will someday rely on those programs shares in the benefit of added solvency.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Social Security payroll tax to wages between the annual cap (roughly $176,000 in 2025) and $400,000 — wages in that range currently pay no Social Security tax at all — so high earners contribute to the program everyone draws from.

Adds a 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 for individuals and $500,000 for joint filers, boosting the hospital insurance fund that pays hospital bills for seniors and disabled people.

Raises taxes on investment income for people earning over $400,000/$500,000: it removes the exemption for active business income from S corporations and partnerships, adds some foreign income, adds a 13.6-percentage-point surtax, and lifts the rate on trusts and estates from 3.8% to 17.4%.

Sends 71.3% of the new investment-income tax to the Social Security old-age and survivors fund, 10.3% to the disability fund, and 28.7% to Medicare's hospital insurance fund, so the money directly supports benefits rather than general spending.

analysis.who_pays: High-income individuals bear the cost: workers and self-employed people earning between the current wage cap and $400,000 (and their employers, who pay a matching share), earners above $400,000/$500,000 who pay the extra 1.2% Medicare tax, and wealthy investors, active business owners, and trusts and estates paying the sharply higher investment-income tax.

drawbacks.text: Employers would owe a matching share of the new Social Security tax on wages between the current cap and $400,000, raising labor costs for businesses with well-paid workers such as medical practices, law firms, and small companies in high-wage areas.

Owners of S corporations and partnerships would pay the new investment-income tax on income from businesses they actively operate — income that has been exempt — and the tax rate for trusts and estates jumps from 3.8% to 17.4%, a steep increase for family trusts.

The extra Social Security taxes paid on wages between the current cap and $400,000 would raise revenue without increasing those taxpayers' own future benefits, since the bill changes no benefit formulas — a fairness objection from the taxpayers who pay in most.

Critics of this approach argue that sharply higher taxes on top earners and investment income can reduce incentives to work, invest, and report income, and that wealthy taxpayers have tools to restructure income to avoid payroll taxes; the bill leaves those avoidance questions to enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — new dedicated revenue for the two programs nearly every American family eventually depends on — is broad, while the cost falls on a small group earning above roughly $400,000 and on wealthy investors and trusts. The main honest criticisms are the added payroll cost on employers for wages between the cap and $400,000, the fact that donut-hole taxes buy the payers no extra benefits, and the risk that sophisticated taxpayers restructure income to escape the new taxes. On balance the design is a deliberate choice to ask the highest earners to fund shared programs, not a hidden transfer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2025 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote; the current Congress runs into January 2027, so it is not officially dead yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced the Medicare and Social Security Fair Share Act on May 8, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law — and no further action of any kind has been taken since.
Not a single House member has signed on as a cosponsor, leaving Boyle as the bill's only supporter in Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, high earners, business owners, and wealthy trusts are better off because the new taxes have not moved; Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries have gained nothing, since no new revenue has been enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors, so far

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and sits in a Republican-run committee, so any partisan shape is inference rather than record.

industries.note: These households would pay the new 1.2% Medicare tax, Social Security tax on wages up to $400,000, and a much larger investment-income tax. Their gain from avoiding these taxes is exactly the revenue the trust funds would have received.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses (S corporations and partnerships)
industries.note: Active business income passed through to high-earning owners is currently exempt from the 3.8% investment-income tax; the bill pulls it in and raises the top rate to 17.4%, ending a long-standing advantage for high-income owners.
The tax rate on undistributed investment income of trusts and estates would jump from 3.8% to 17.4%, a nearly fivefold increase concentrated on accumulated family wealth.

industries.industry: Employers with workers earning between the wage cap and $400,000
industries.note: Employers pay a matching share of Social Security tax, so they would owe an additional 6.2% on wages between roughly $176,000 and $400,000, a real cost increase for firms with higher-paid professionals.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action more than half a year after introduction, and a Ways and Means calendar controlled by the opposing party, the bill is on a well-worn path to dying in committee when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, as similar Social Security funding proposals from previous congresses have.
